newsitem.title: USA: U.S. reports decline in tuberculosis cases.
newsitem.headline: U.S. reports decline in tuberculosis cases.

text.p: The number of new cases of tuberculosis in the United States decreased for the fourth consecutive year in 1996, with New York City leading the way in fighting the disease, officials said on Monday.

The announcement at a news conference in Harlem, historically a community hard hit by tuberculosis, followed a report last week by the World Health Organisation (WHO) that said a new strategy in treatment could save millions of lives worldwide.

"The data demonstrates that this disease is still very much with us but that we are on the right track," Dr. Kenneth Castro, director of the divison of TB elimination at the U.S. Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, told reporters at Harlem Hospital.

"For the fourth year in a row, the number of tuberculosis cases has declined in the United States ... this recovery shows how important it is for us to learn from our past mistakes and to continue to fight relentlessly to eliminate tuberculosis in the United States," he said.

Castro said the number of TB cases in 1996 decreased 6.7 percent to 21,327 cases from 22,860 cases in 1995. New York officials, at the same news conference, also reported a fourth consecutive year of decline -- 2,053 new cases in 1996 compared with 2,445 in 1995.

New York accounted for 26 percent of the decrease in all TB cases reported across the country, city officials said. There were 14 years of increases in new TB patients in the city before the decline began 4 years ago.

"It is imperative that we continue to provide adequate resources to control TB," New York City Health Commissioner Margaret Hamburg said. "In the 1960s and '70s, we made the mistake of thinking that TB could not resurface in America and we allowed the resources and infrastructure that had been built up to decline."
The WHO said last Wednesday that the administration of Directly Observed Treatment Short-course, or DOTS, was causing the worldwide TB epidemic to level off for the first time in decades.

DOTS calls for training health workers or community members to counsel and observe patients to insure they take the standard four antibiotics, not only until symptoms disappear but until they are cured.

The WHO programme could also dramatically reduce the threat of the emergence of TB bacilli resistant to drugs, and could cut long-term costs, representatives from the United Nations health agency said.

WHO said nearly three million people died from the disease last year, more people than at the epidemic's height in the first part of the century, when it swept across North America and Europe, killing one out of every seven people.
